content: Carbonic anhydrase 14 is an enzyme encoded by the CA14 gene in humans. Carbonic anhydrases (CAs) are a large family of zinc-containing metalloenzymes that facilitate the reversible hydration of carbon dioxide into bicarbonate and protons. These enzymes are involved in numerous physiological processes, including respiration, regulation of acid-base balance, calcification, bone resorption, and the production of aqueous humor, cerebrospinal fluid, saliva, and gastric acid. Carbonic anhydrases exhibit significant diversity in their distribution across different tissues and in their subcellular localization. CA XIV is predicted to function as a type I membrane protein. It shares the highest sequence similarity with another transmembrane carbonic anhydrase isoform, CA XII. Despite this similarity, CA XIV and CA XII have distinct patterns of tissue-specific expression, suggesting that they may serve different physiological roles. In melanocytic cells, the expression of the CA14 gene may be regulated by the microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF), which is known to play a critical role in melanocyte development and function.
